headline: Spin models with three or more components are proved to lose alignment exponentially at every temperature.
scope: Nearest-neighbor O(n) models on the square grid: n ≥ 3 for decay, n = 4 for the mass, n = 3 for the continuum.
plain: Put a unit arrow at each point of a flat grid, with neighbors preferring to align. With three or more components per arrow, this paper family proves the alignment fades exponentially with distance at every temperature. For four components it claims the exact fading rate at low temperature. For three components it claims a continuum quantum field theory with a mass gap.
doesNot: This does not give a Lean check of the O(4) mass formula or the O(3) continuum theory, and it says nothing new about two-component spins.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Alexander Polyakov, the prediction of mass generation
scorecard.significanceWhy: It would settle a long-standing question about two-dimensional spin models, with a Lean proof of the decay part.

explanation:
Take two arrows of length one that can point anywhere in three-dimensional space. Let them prefer to line up, with a strength called β. Pick their directions at random, weighted by e raised to β times the dot product of the two arrows. The dot product is 1 when they align and −1 when they oppose. At β = 1, the average dot product works out to coth(1) − 1, about 0.313. So the two arrows are mildly aligned.

Now place such an arrow at every point of a flat square grid, with each neighbor pair preferring to align. This is the O(n) model, where n is the number of components of each arrow. For n = 3 it is the classical Heisenberg magnet. The question is how fast the alignment between two distant arrows fades with distance. In two dimensions there is no lasting order at any temperature[1]. But that leaves open whether the fading is exponential or slower[2].

For n = 2 the fading can be slow, by a polynomial law at low temperature[3]. For three or more components, Polyakov's argument predicted exponential fading at every positive temperature[4]. Rigorous results covered only high temperature or very many components[5]. Aru, Garban and Sepúlveda recorded the all-temperature question as open in 2025[6].

This family of five papers claims several answers. One paper proves exponential fading for every n of at least 3 and every temperature[7]. The bound is uniform over finite pieces of the grid with free edges[8]. For n = 4, another paper claims the exact rate at low temperature. The mass, the inverse of the fading length, behaves like 32·e^(π/4 − 1/2)·√β·e^(−πβ) as β grows[9]. The prefactor 32·e^(π/4 − 1/2) is about 42.57. At β = 2 the formula gives a mass near 0.112, a fading length near 9 grid steps. At β = 3 the length is near 168 steps. These numbers come from the leading formula, which is exact only in the limit. A companion paper claims upper and lower bounds of the same shape, and a positive gap at every temperature[10].

For n = 3, the remaining papers claim a continuum limit. Shrink the grid spacing while β grows, keeping a physical length fixed. The limit exists along every value of β, without choosing a subsequence[11]. It defines a genuine interacting quantum field theory with a positive mass gap[12]. Its lightest particle shows up as an isolated point in the spectrum[13].

The single obstacle is the low-temperature regime. There the fading length is exponentially large, and the system looks ordered over huge distances. Earlier bounds by McBryan and Spencer gave only polynomial fading, which allows a zero exponential rate[2]. A mass estimate on a fixed grid also does not by itself give the continuum theory[14].

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has a formal proof of exponential fading on finite grid pieces. It covers every n of at least 3 and every temperature. The infinite-grid limit, the O(4) mass results and the O(3) continuum construction lie outside that check. No specialist review of any of the five papers has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if it holds. Exponential decay on finite grid pieces has a Lean proof; the O(4) mass asymptotic and the O(3) continuum theory do not. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A grid of unit arrows with n components, where neighboring arrows prefer to align.
The strength of the preference to align; large β means low temperature.
Correlation falling at least as fast as a constant times e^(−m·distance), for some m > 0.
A positive rate m of exponential decay; its inverse is the correlation length.
The theory obtained as the grid spacing shrinks to zero while a physical length stays fixed.
No arrows are fixed at the edge of the finite grid piece.

claims.sourceLine: nearest-neighbor $O(n)$ model on the square lattice, for every $n\ge3$
claims.sourceQuote: We prove exponential decay of two-point correlations for the classical nearest-neighbor $O(n)$ model on the square lattice, for every $n\ge3$ and every finite positive inverse temperature.

claims.sourceQuote: The estimate is uniform over finite free-boundary subgraphs and bounded nonnegative edge strengths.

claims.sourceQuote: For the nearest-neighbor \(O(4)\) model on the square lattice at inverse temperature \(\beta\), we prove the exact low-temperature asymptotic \[ m_{\mathrm{lat}}(\beta)\sim 32\exp(\pi/4-1/2)\sqrt\beta\,\exp(-\pi\beta) \qquad (\beta\to\infty). \]

claims.text: The O(4) full gap is bounded by multiples of sqrt(beta)e^{-pi beta}, with a positive gap at every beta.
claims.sourceQuote: We also prove that the model has a unique periodic local limit and a positive full gap at every finite $\beta>0$, resolving the all-temperature lattice mass-generation conjecture for this periodic state.

claims.sourceQuote: We consider the continuum spin field constructed from the nearest-neighbor two-dimensional $O(3)$ model by the fixed prescription of the companion paper. We prove that its vector two-point spectral measure has a positive atom corresponding to the lowest mass, separated by a positive gap from all remaining mass support.
